segments.text:
Hello everyone. Welcome back to Altium 
Academy. I'm your host, Zach Peterson.

Today we're going to be doing a little 
follow-up video to our recent video about

decoupling capacitor placement and why 
it is less important when you're using

planes versus using traces. Now, this 
follow-up video was all spawned by a

message I received from a viewer through 
LinkedIn. And this message specifically

concerns the use of traces versus vias 
to make connections to power and ground

nets when placing and connecting decoupling 
capacitors to integrated circuits.

As we go through this question, we're 
going to take a look at some examples in

Altium Designer and we're going to see 
what real pinouts look like and how they

can sometimes constrain capacitor placement 
and force you to use one connection

type over the other. Let's go 
ahead and jump in and get started.
Now, this video

is a great followup to our previous video 
about decoupling capacitor placement

and whether or not it is really sensitive 
to location when you're using planes

to route power and ground into an 
integrated circuit, particularly a large

integrated circuit that uses a BGA 
package. Now, if you haven't watched that

video, make sure to check out the video 
link in the description and go watch

that video before we continue here. Now, 
if you have watched that video, you'll

know that we arrived at two important 
conclusions about the location of

decoupling capacitors around large 
integrated circuits. The first is that if you

have a BGA package and you have to use 
power planes and ground planes to route

power into that BGA, the location of the 
decoupling capacitor is less important

when the planes are very large. That's 
because the connection between the

decoupling capacitor and that BGA has 
very low inductance and it's much lower

inductance than if you were to use traces 
to connect the pads of the decoupling

capacitor into the pins on the BGA. But 
the second thing that we saw which is

much more important is that when we 
have a BGA package, it's generally

impossible to make that connection using 
traces because the power and ground

pins tend to be clustered in the center 
of the BGA package rather than around

the edge. Now in that situation where 
you have a package where the leads are

located around the edge of the package, 
it is possible to bring a decoupling

capacitor very close to the leads and 
make the trace connection. But what we

didn't address in that other video was 
how we make the connection back to the

power and ground net in the PCB. Should 
we use vias and connect directly to the

power and ground planes? What if we don't 
have a power plane and we only have a

ground plane? Should we just use a long 
trace routing over to the power net?

These are all important questions that 
we didn't address in the other video and

they came up recently in this LinkedIn 
question that was sent to me by Peter

Barnes. Let's take a look at Peter's 
LinkedIn question. Peter writes, "Hi Zach,

I was at a Würth/Analog Devices seminar 
the other day and the FAE from Analog

Devices referenced his comment on this 
LinkedIn post." And here he gives us the

link to that LinkedIn comment. I did my 
best to convince him at the time that

you are better off with a ground via 
for every decoupling capacitor and solid

reference planes, but I don't think I 
managed to change his mind. He was also

recommending analog ground islands under 
DCDC converters, which I know for sure

is a bad idea. Well, Peter, you are 
absolutely correct about that. Perhaps you

could reply to his comment. He does say 
that he would welcome a good argument.

Well, you all know I like to argue with 
people on LinkedIn, but sometimes it's

more fun to start the argument on YouTube. 
So before we go further, let's take a

look at this post and comment. So this 
post came up from Ömer Faruk DEMİRTAŞ.

Here he's showing what happens when you 
place a decoupling capacitor and then

make some connections back to the power 
nets. He details a correct way to do it

and an incorrect way to do it. In reality, 
they're both incorrect because he's

placing ferrite beads on the power 
nets, but let's just ignore that for the

moment because I've explained that 
one to death. Let's just focus on the

placement of the decoupling capacitor 
on the positive voltage net and then the

ground pin over here on the bottom side 
of the IC. So basically what Omar is

saying is that the correct way to do 
this is to use individual vias on the

ground pin and then on the grounded pad 
on the decoupling capacitor whereas the

incorrect way to do this would be to 
route this long trace from the decoupling

capacitor pad over to this via and then 
share that via between the decoupling

capacitor net and this ground pin on 
the IC. Now, the comment Peter Barnes is

referencing is right here from Simon 
Bramble. And Simon writes, "M, I am not so

sure this is correct. A PCB trace 
generally has a lower inductance than a PCB

via. And you need to keep the inductance 
low to maintain the high frequency

performance of the capacitor. A PCB trace 
has a return path through the ground

plane, which keeps its inductance small 
unless the ground plane is several

layers below the trace. In addition, 
you are decoupling the whole device, not

just the V+ pin. The power supply that 
the device sees is the one between its V+

and ground pins. So, it is this voltage 
that needs to be decoupled, not V+ to

any local ground node that might be at 
a different potential to the ground pin.

So, we're going to investigate Simon's 
statements just a little bit inside of

Altium Designer by looking at a couple 
of real components and the location of

their power and ground pins. And then we 
can understand a little bit better what

are the optimal ways to make those 
connections because sometimes it's not just

about the inductance. It's actually 
about what type of connection method is

practical given the location of those 
pins on the integrated circuit. Now,

before we investigate these statements 
from Simon Bramble, what I want to do is

take a look at a couple of real components 
that have the leads exposed around

the edge of the package and with the 
power and ground pins in different

locations. This is going to help us see 
how we might have to place and route the

connections from the decoupling capacitor 
into those power and ground pins based

on the location of those pins in the 
package. So, here I have our Ethernet

switch project pulled up and we're going 
to look at two memories that we have

placed in this design. And if you're 
interested in learning more about this

design, you can go and access the design 
files from the link in the description.

You can also see a link to a video where 
we go over the design for this Ethernet

switch. So here we're going to look at 
the SPI Flash. And you can see here we

have a power pin and a ground pin. So we 
have a single power pin, single ground

pin on pin two and pin 10. And then we're 
also going to look at the NAND flash.

This NAND flash has two power pins and 
two ground pins. And you can see that we

have a decoupling capacitor right here 
linking them. So now let's take a look at

these packages in the PCB layout. Here 
you can see we have the larger NAND flash

and then that one decoupling capacitor 
is located right here. And then here we

have the smaller SPI Flash. And then it 
also has a decoupling capacitor which is

located right here between pin 2 and 
ground. So first let's look at the smaller

SPI flash. So here on this SPI Flash, 
you can see here that we have our power

pin right here on pin two and then we 
have our ground pin all the way over here

on pin 10. So they're on opposite sides 
of the package. Now if we just go back

over here to this post on LinkedIn and 
then we just scroll up here to the image

from Omar, this situation looks a lot 
like the image on the left where we have a

lot of distance in between the power pin 
and the ground pin. Now here, Omar says

that the correct way to do this is to 
put a via to the ground plane right here

on the ground pin and then put a via 
to the ground plane right here on the

negative side of this decoupling capacitor. 
Now here in the PCB layout, you'll

see that we do have a via going into the 
ground plane, but then we also have a

via going into the power plane. So the 
question is, is it better to place these

vias connecting to the planes rather than 
routing a trace from the ground pin on

the capacitor all the way over here 
to this ground pin on the integrated

circuit? Well, I think the answer is 
obviously yes. This is clearly better. It's

better just from a placement and routing 
perspective. Why would you route a big

trace all the way up here and take up 
all that space when you have a convenient

connection to ground through a via 
both on this pin and on this pin on the

decoupling capacitor? So to me it seems 
obvious that when you have the power pin

and the ground pin placed far away from 
each other, the optimal way to do this

in terms of convenience of routing is 
to just use vias to connect back to the

plane. Now let's go back and take a look 
at Simon Bramble's statement here in

the comments. So, Simon Bramble says 
that I am not so sure this is correct. A

PCB trace generally has a lower inductance 
than a PCB via and you need to keep

the inductance low to maintain the high 
frequency performance of the capacitor.

Well, what we saw in our earlier video 
on decoupling capacitor placement was

that it is true. You do need to keep 
the inductance low to maintain the high

frequency performance of the capacitor 
just like Simon says right here in this

sentence. So that is a true statement. 
What is not a true statement is this part

of the sentence which is that a PCB trace 
generally has a lower inductance than

the PCB via that is actually not true. 
It is only true when traces are very

short and the reason is that traces have 
an inductance per unit length. We can

actually calculate what that inductance 
per unit length is inside the Layer

Stack Manager inside Altium. So here 
inside the Layer Stack Manager you can see

that we have the impedance tab brought 
up and over here on the right hand side

we can see that we have an impedance 
calculation and it gives us the inductance

per unit length and you can see here 
that the inductance of this 6.1 mil trace

which is a 50 ohm trace for a DK4 
laminate is 7.85 nanohenries per inch. Now

just a rough estimate of the distance in 
between this power pin and this ground

pin is about half an inch. So this would 
be about a 3.9 nanohenry connection

just between this capacitor and this 
ground pin on this integrated circuit. Well

that 3.9 nanohenries is about four 
times as large as a typical PCB via that

would connect back to the ground plane. 
So clearly in this case where you have

the power pin and the ground pin at a 
very large distance from each other using

a trace is not optimal from the 
inductance perspective as well as from the

routing convenience perspective. That 
trace connection is always going to have a

higher inductance than the via connection 
back to that plane. And that's why in

this situation with this type of chip 
on screen, we would prefer to always use

the vias to make the connection back 
to the planes rather than routing a big

trace all the way from the decoupling 
capacitor pin over to the integrated

circuit pin. Now let's take a look at 
the other memory that we have in this

design. So you can see that this chip 
is right here. We have a decoupling

capacitor placed right here in between 
the power pin and the ground pin. So you

can see very clearly the power pin and 
the ground pin are right next to each

other. Now, it's worth asking in this 
case, is it better to route traces

directly from the capacitor to the 
pins? Or instead of using these traces,

should we then also just put a via right 
here that connects from the internal

plane directly to the pins? So, for 
example, should we do something like this

with the 3.3 volt net? And then should 
we also do something like this with the

ground net? Well, here in this connection 
where I've just quickly placed these

vias on the 3.3 volt net and the ground 
net, we have a via going from the 3.3

volt pin into the plane and then coming 
back up through another via and then

going into the pin. So that's approximately 
2 nanohenries of inductance from

those two vias. I haven't included the 
trace impedance because as you can see

here the traces are very short only 
about 1 millimeter in length. Same thing

here for the ground connection. We'd have 
one nanohenry of inductance here from

this via and approximately another 
nanohenry of inductance from this via.

However, if we just make the connection 
using the traces as we had originally,

we would have much lower inductance. 
Here you can see that we would have a

distance of about 70 mil. So that's a 
much lower inductance connection when we

can route these traces directly from 
the decoupling capacitor over to these

pins. The only reason we're able to get 
such a low inductance connection in this

case is because the power and ground 
pins are literally right next to each

other. And that's what allows us to place 
that decoupling capacitor very close

and route in with these very short 
traces. So to summarize, should you use

traces on every pin or should you use 
vias on every pin to make connections

between decoupling capacitor pins and 
integrated circuit power and ground pins?

Well, it depends. Where are the pins 
located? How far apart are they? Are they

located right next to each other? And 
can you bring that decoupling capacitor

very close and make those trace connections? 
Those are the types of questions

that you need to ask. And unfortunately, 
that context is not clear if you just

take a look at the image provided by Omar 
on that LinkedIn post. Hopefully, this

adds just the right context that you 
need to understand decoupling capacitor

placement and power integrity, specifically 
in the case of integrated circuit

packages where the leads are located 
around the edge of the package. Thanks for

watching this video everybody and of 
course don't be afraid to send me your

questions on LinkedIn or of course you 
can hop into the comment section and

leave your comments and questions 
there. Don't forget to subscribe to the

channel and don't forget to call your 
fabricator folks. We'll see you next time.

title: Decoupling Capacitor Routing: When to Use Vias vs Traces
